rendering.persona_description: Farid is a 67-year-old retired shop teacher who spent thirty years teaching woodworking and small-engine repair at a vocational high school. He's married to his wife of 34 years, keeps a workbench in the garage, and still does small repair jobs for neighbors. He's a plain, practical man who doesn't like a fuss made over him.
rendering.clinical_context: Farid has a specific phobia of needles and blood draws that goes back to childhood, worse than ordinary nerves: he has fainted or come close to fainting more than once at the sight of a needle. Because of it he avoided routine bloodwork for years and switched from testosterone injections to a gel decades ago rather than deal with needles regularly. His doctor pushed for more frequent labs as he's gotten older, so he started exposure therapy about six weeks ago and is working through a hierarchy: photos of needles, videos of blood draws, holding a capped syringe, and now a scheduled mock blood draw at the clinic.
rendering.behavioral_description: Farid talks in short, practical sentences and tends to downplay how bad the fear actually gets, saying things like 'it's not that big a deal' right after describing nearly passing out. He goes along easily with whatever is suggested, saying 'sure, I can try that' without much pushback, but he doesn't always follow through fully once he's on his own. He'd rather talk about the logistics of an exposure exercise than how he feels about it.
